titleStmt.title: A Cognac-Glass Algorithm for Conditionally Guaranteed Budgets

analytic.title: A Cognac-Glass Algorithm for Conditionally Guaranteed Budgets

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: To analyse the schedulability of conditionally guaranteed budgets (CGBs) in the context of fixed-priority preemptive scheduling (FPPS), we present a so-called cognacglass algorithm (CGA).

CGBs have been conceived in the context of software video processing for consumer terminals to exploit the relative importance of applications. CGBs are similar to normal budgets, but are only conditionally guaranteed. This paper presents the schedulability analysis of CGBs under FPPS, based on both best-case and worst-case analysis techniques. We show that because both techniques are used, it is not straightforward to base the analysis on a critical instant. We therefore have to investigate multiple phasings of budgets during the analysis, for which we present a socalled cognac-glass algorithm. We derive that it suffices to consider only a subset of so-called dominating values for the phasing, which improves the efficiency of our algorithm.

Given our analysis, we evaluate the effectiveness of CGBs, and conclude that CGBs are particularly useful for software video processing. Finally, we briefly compare our approach for CGBs with existing analysis techniques for hierarchical FPPS, and illustrate that best-case analysis techniques and a CGA can reduce the inherent pessimism in these existing techniques.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Software video processing is often characterized by highly fluctuating, content dependent, resource requirements that are not known a priori. Typically, there is a large gap between the worst-case and average-case processing time. Because consumer terminals, such as digital TV-sets and set-top boxes, have a high pressure on cost and power consumption, resource allocation has to be close to averagecase, and some form of load reduction is inevitable to prevent overload. On the other hand, high-quality video has stringent jitter requirements, i.e. deadline misses are considered as severe failures. Fortunately, perception is key for consumer terminals providing high-quality video processing, and the notion of Quality of Service (QoS) can therefore be fruitfully applied to reduce load. To prevent temporal interference between applications upon overloads, resource allocation can be based on guaranteed periodic CPU budgets.

In [19], QoS control strategies for high-quality video are presented, that allow close-to-average resource allocation and operate with a given budget, based on asynchronous, scalable processing, and QoS adaptation. The approach can be complemented with a mechanism for budget control that exploits the notion of relative importance of applications [4]. This mechanism supports maintaining a stable output quality of a more important application (MIA) upon a structural load increase, at the cost of having to revert to best-effort approaches for quality degradation of a predetermined set of less important applications (LIAs). The mechanism facilitates an anticipated, instantaneous budget increase for MIA, and is based on the concept of a conditionally guaranteed budget (CGB). To distinguish a normal budget from a CGB, we sometimes use the term absolutely guaranteed budget (AGB).

In a basic setting of a system with CGBs, we consider a set A of independent applications that are executed on a shared resource and two sets B N and B A of periodic budgets. The set A consists of a single MIA, a single LIA, and other, neutral applications. Although we consider only a single tuple consisting of a single MIA and a single LIA, our results equally well apply to multiple tuples, each consisting of a MIA and one or more LIAs. Each budget of B N as well as B A is allocated and provided to a specific application, where the sets B N and B A only differ in the budgets for MIA and LIA. The sets B N and B A correspond to a normal (low) load for MIA and an anticipated high load for MIA, respectively. Both sets facilitate the same normal budgets for both MIA and LIA. B A facilitates the additional resources for MIA, a so-called budget margin. B N facilitates an additional CGB for LIA, which is based on the budget margin of MIA. To prevent a temporary overload situation upon an instantaneous budget configuration change from B N to B A , in-the-place-of resource provision is applied for the CGB [4], i.e. the CGB is provided at the period and phasing of the budget margin, and when the budget margin would have been provided.

The problem to be addressed for the analysis of CGBs is to determine the worst-case amount of resources, i.e. the highest lower bound, that can be conditionally guaranteed to LIA at the period and phasing of its normal budget given the budget margin for MIA.

In this paper, we describe the analysis of CGBs in the context of fixed-priority preemptive scheduling (FPPS), based on best-case and worst-case analysis techniques. We observe that the basic setting of a system with CGBs is a special case of a system with two-level hierarchical scheduling on a shared resource, with budgets at the global level and applications at the local level [6,15].

div.head: Related work
div.p: The need for best-case analysis techniques for FPPS has been previously identified in the area of jitter in general and in the area of distributed systems in particular [5,8,13,14]. Because the resources of budgets become available with jitter due to interference with higher priority budgets, our work builds on those earlier results.

Response time analysis of systems based on two-level hierarchical FPPS has been addressed in [1,3,6,15,17]. In these papers, each application consists of a set of tasks and a separate budget is allocated to each application. Below, we focus on [6], because its schedulability test improves on the earlier work. Main focus of the analysis in [6] is on the worst-case response times of tasks. The analysis is based on a so-called critical instant for a task, which is defined as the pattern of execution of other tasks and budgets that leads to the worst-case response time of that task. The analysis uses sophisticated worst-case analysis techniques, but only a rudimentary form of a best-case analysis technique.
In this paper, we show that because we use both best-case and worst-case analysis techniques, it is not straightforward to base the analysis on a critical instant.

div.head: Overview
div.p: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We start by giving a scheduling model for CGBs in Section 2 and explaining the essentials of CGBs. In Section 3, we briefly describe basic best-case and worst-case analysis techniques that we need to analyse a system with CGBs in the context of FPPS. We recapitulate response times, briefly describe so-called occupied times and advancements, and complement best-case analysis with similar techniques as developed for worst-case analysis. The analysis of CGBs by means of a cognac-glass algorithm (CGA) is the topic of Section 4. In Section 5, we evaluate the effectiveness of CGBs, and briefly compare our CGA approach with existing analysis techniques for hierarchical scheduling under FPPS. Finally, we conclude the paper in Section 6.

div.head: A scheduling model for CGBs
div.p: This section presents a real-time scheduling model for CGBs, providing a basis for the analysis of CGBs. We start with a basic scheduling model for budgets. Next, we recapitulate CGBs and present inherent budget configurations for CGBs. We subsequently discuss budget guarantees for both normal budgets and CGBs upon a budget configuration change, and describe a concept that prevents an overload during such a change. A description of the two main steps to analyse a system with CGBs concludes the section.

div.head: Basic scheduling model for budgets
div.p: In essence, a budget may simply be viewed as an artificial task, and all notions for real-time tasks can be reused for budgets. The fact that budgets are allocated and provided to applications is not important for our model for budgets.

We assume a single processor, and a set B of n independent periodic budgets, denoted by β 1 , β 2 , ...β n . At any moment in time, the processor is used to 'provide' the highest priority budget that has not been depleted. Similarly to [6], we assume that a budget is never discarded or suspended. Budgets are ready for consumption, i.e. they are replenished, when activated (or released) and consumption is not suspended. An activation of a budget is also termed a job. When a budget β i is being consumed, and a release occurs for a higher priority budget β j , then the consumption of β i is preempted instantaneously, and will resume when the consumption of β j has ended, as well as all other releases of budgets with a higher priority than β i that have taken place in the meanwhile. Similarly to real-time tasks, each budget β i is characterized by a (release) period T i ∈ R + , a capacity C i ∈ R + , a (relative) deadline D i ∈ R + , and a phasing ϕ i ∈ R, where ϕ i serves as a reference replenishment. The combination of phasings ϕ i is termed the phasing ϕ of the budget set B. We assume that capacities C i are fixed and deadlines D i are hard, i.e. when a budget β i is replenished upon its activation, it must be depleted before the corresponding deadline. Moreover, we assume deadlines equal to periods, i.e. D i = T i , arbitrary phasing, and unique priorities in this paper. For notational convenience, we assume that budget β j has a higher priority than budget β i if and only if j < i. As mentioned before, we assume an FPPS model for budgets, and therefore allow an arbitrary assignment of priorities to budgets.

div.head: Recapitulation of CGBs
div.p: As indicated before, MIA instantaneously receives a budget margin upon request to accommodate an anticipated structural load increase, allowing MIA to maintain an acceptable perceived quality level. This budget margin of MIA can be accommodated by giving LIA a lower budget. To gain back on cost-effectiveness loss and to compensate LIA for its budget loss, LIA receives an additional budget with a conditional guarantee, based on a conditional admission test. This so-called conditionally guaranteed budget (CGB) is available to LIA when MIA does not use its budget margin, and is based on that margin.

The resource manager provides dedicated means for CGBs that allow MIA to voluntarily restrain its budget use, i.e. MIA explicitly claims and releases its budget margin based on its resource needs. These claims and releases cause the withdrawal and provision of the CGB to LIA, respectively, and LIA is explicitly informed about this change. LIA can therefore count on its CGB during the interval of time from the moment that MIA releases its budget margin to the moment MIA re-claims it.

div.head: Budget configurations for CGBs
div.p: Consider two budget configurations, a normal configuration B N and an anticipated configuration B A corresponding to a normal (low) load for MIA and a high load for MIA, respectively. These two configurations correspond to two modes in which the system can run, a normal mode and an anticipated mode. B N facilitates a normal budget β M for MIA and a normal budget β L plus a conditionally guaranteed budget β c L for LIA. β M is characterized by a three-tuple < T M ,C M , ϕ M >. β L and β c L are characterized by < T L ,C L , ϕ L > and < T L , ∆C L , ϕ L >, respectively. Note that β L and β c L have the same period T L and phasing ϕ L . Hence, a capacity C L + ∆C L is provided to LIA at a period T L and phasing ϕ L in normal mode. B A facilitates an anticipated budget β M for MIA and just the normal budget
div.formula: β L for LIA. β M is characterized by < T M ,C M + ∆C M , ϕ M >, i.e. β M
div.p: includes an additional capacity ∆C M , the so-called capacity margin, representing the budget margin. Note that we make no assumptions about the periods T M and T L , i.e. our results hold for T M < T L , T M = T L , as well as for T M > T L .
The budgets of other, neutral applications are the same for both configurations.

div.head: Budget configuration changes
div.p: The difference between an AGB and a CGB becomes apparent upon a change from B N to B A . As mentioned before, MIA causes such a change by (re-)claiming its capacity margin. Upon such a change, all AGBs remain guaranteed. Moreover, MIA is guaranteed to receive its entire capacity margin instantaneously, i.e. as from the budget period in which it claimed it, under the condition that it was still consuming the β M part upon the claim. Unlike AGBs, a CGB is not guaranteed upon such a change, and a CGB may even be withdrawn in the midst of its consumption.

div.head: In-the-place-of resource provision
div.p: Without precautionary measures, an instantaneous budget configuration change from B N to B A may cause a temporary overload situation, potentially jeopardizing the guarantees of AGBs [16]. Such an overload situation can be prevented by making sure that a CGB is never consumed before the corresponding capacity margin on which it is based would have been consumed. This can be accomplished by applying the so-called concept of in-the-place-of resource provision for CGB consumption [4], i.e. the CGB β c L is consumed at the period and phasing of the budget β M , and when the capacity margin ∆C M would have been consumed. A conceivable implementation of this concept is to provide β c L at an intermediate priority just below the priority of β M .

div.head: Schedulability analysis
div.p: To analyse a system with CGBs, we first determine the schedulability of the anticipated budget configuration B A , for which we can use standard analysis techniques for FPPS. Next, we need to determine the worst-case amount of capacity ∆C L that can be conditionally guaranteed to LIA at the period and phasing of β L for the normal budget configuration B N . For in-the-place-of resource provision, β c L becomes available at the period and phasing of β M , and when ∆C M would have become available. We therefore need a conversion from < T M , ∆C M , ϕ M > to < T L , ∆C L , ϕ L > for the analysis of CGBs. Hence, we need to determine the highest lower bound of the amount of capacity margin ∆C M that becomes available in an interval of length T L with an arbitrary relative phasing ϕ R of β L with respect to β M . How to compute this, is the main topic of this paper.

div.head: Occupied times
div.p: The occupied time O ik of a job k of a budget β i is closely related to its response time R ik . The occupied time of a job of β i is defined as the length of the interval from the release of that job during which the processor is occupied with the provision of its capacity C i and provisions of higher priority budgets until the moment in time that the same job could start an additional bit of computation. Hence, the occupied time includes preemptions and aligning successive provisions of higher priority budgets.

The worst-case occupied time WO i under arbitrary phasing is the longest occupied time. Note that we only consider a single job of β i for the worst-case occupied time, making our notion different from the notion of busy period [10]. To determine worst-case occupied times under arbitrary phasing, we can use a similar approach as for worstcase response times. The main difference between both approaches is that aligning successive provisions of higher priority budgets also have to be taken into account when determining WO i . For the construction of WO i by means of a time line, this is illustrated in Figure 1 for budget β M . div.head: Advancement
div.p: The advancement A i (t) of a budget β i in a time interval of length t starting at a release of β i is the amount of capacity that has been provided in that interval. Note that the advancement of a budget β i may be viewed as the inverse of the response time of that budget. The best-case advancement BA i (t) of β i in an interval of length t starting at a release of β i is the maximal amount of capacity that can be provided in that interval. BA i (t) is given by

div.head: Determining advancement graphs
div.p: The graphs for BA i (t) and WA i (t) are characterized by their bending points, and we can therefore determine an advancement graph by calculating its bending points. We will illustrate how bending points in the graphs for BA i (t) and WA i (t) can be calculated for the example given above.

We mention that the technique to determine bending points for WA i (t) is similar to the technique to determine spare capacity [9]. We start at t = 0, and observe that WA M (0) = 0 by definition. The graph for WA M (t) has a horizontal line-segment for 0 ≤ t ≤ WO M (0), and a WObending point is therefore found for t = WO M (0) = 3. The next bending point is a WR-bending point, which is found at the end of a diagonal line-segment that starts at WO M (0), i.e. which is found at t = WR M (3) = 6. This point can be determined using a so-called first scheduling point [9]. div.head: Analysis of CGBs under FPPS using a CGA
div.p: As mentioned before, the problem to be addressed for the analysis of CGBs is to determine the worst-case amount of capacity ∆C L that can be conditionally guaranteed to LIA on the periodic and phasing of β L . Hence, we need to determine the highest lower bound of the amount of capacity margin ∆C M that becomes available in an interval of length T L with an arbitrary relative phasing ϕ R of β L with respect to β M .

The earliest and latest times that ∆C M becomes available under arbitrary phasing after a release of β M are the length of shortest and longest intervals of time from a release of β M to the start of the execution of ∆C M , i.e. BO M (C M ) and WO M (C M ), respectively; see Figure 4. Similarly, the earliest and latest times that ∆C M is depleted under arbitrary phasing after a release of β M are given by BR M (C M + ∆C M ) and WR M (C M + ∆C M ), respectively. Hence, ∆C M becomes available with jitter due to the fact that it has to wait until the C M part has finished, which may suffer from preemptions by higher priority budgets.
The relative phasing ϕ R is given by
div.formula: ϕ R = (ϕ L -ϕ M ) mod T M . (9
div.p: Note that 0 ≤ ϕ R < T M . For harmonic periods, i.e. T L = mT M for some m ∈ N + , the relative phasing of every activation of β L is equal to ϕ R . Hence, when ϕ R is known, an amount ∆C L = m∆C M can be conditionally guaranteed if

div.head: A cognac-glass algorithm for CGBs
div.p: Figure 6 shows an expedient based on ∆C B L (t) and ∆C W L (t -T M ) that can be used to determine ∆C L using a so-called cognac glass algorithm (CGA). For a particular value of T L belonging to sub-domain (ii), this algorithm takes the minimum of ∆C L (ϕ R , T L ) for the values of the relative phasing ϕ R for which T L has an overlap with l = 2 T M -intervals. The term CGA originates from the observation that the slanted lines may be viewed as the shape of a glass, and the minimum sum of the height of the cognac at both sides of the glass when tilting the glass determines the capacity for a specific period The result of applying this algorithm is shown in Figure 9. An efficient algorithm to determine ∆C L (T L ) is the topic of the next section.

div.head: Effectiveness of CGBs under FPPS
div.p: We define the effectiveness of CGBs as the ratio between the worst-case available ∆C L (T L ) and the amount ∆C We now evaluate the effectiveness of CGBs for our example. Figure 9 also shows ∆C avg L (T L ). The gap between ∆C avg L (T L ) and ∆C L (T L ) for a particular T L represents the amount of budget margin that cannot be conditionally guaranteed to LIA, and can therefore only be provided as gain time. Because the shape of ∆C L (T L ) is periodic and the (periodic) growth of ∆C L (T L ) is equal to the gradient of ∆C avg L (T L ), this gap is also periodic (with period T M ). Based on this figure, we conclude that the effectiveness of CGBs is small for small values of T L and increases for values of T L in an interval around (a multiple of) T M . This latter conclusion is attractive for the software video processing domain, because applications are typically harmonic, e.g. a 50Hz LIA and a 100Hz MIA.

div.head: Existing analysis of hierarchical FPPS
div.p: As illustrated in [5], a best-case advancement can be directly followed by a worst-case advancement. In general, however, Lemma 1 need not yield a tight bound on the worst-case available capacity, and our analytical results are therefore typically pessimistic.

The assumptions concerning worst-case availability of capacity made by existing analysis techniques for hierarchical FPPS [1,6,15] are similar to our Lemma 1. However, whereas the existing techniques assume that the capacity becomes available without preemptions and as early as possible in best-case situations, our analysis is based on bestcase analysis techniques. The main advantage of the pessimistic assumption in existing work is that a unique critical instant can be assumed, whereas in our case the worst-case available capacity depends on T L , and we therefore have to apply a CGA. The main disadvantage of the assumption in existing work is that it is too pessimistic, in particular for normalized values of T L belonging to sub-domain (ii). This is illustrated in Figure 9, where the dashed line shows the worst-case available capacity ∆C L (T L ) based on the assumptions made in [6].

Because the existing analysis techniques for hierarchical FPPS are based on pessimistic assumptions, we claim that best-case analysis techniques and a CGA are valuable extensions. To substantiate our claim, we will revisit our example and look at it from a two-level hierarchical FPPS perspective. Let MIA consist of two tasks τ 1 and τ 2 , where τ 1 has a higher priority than τ 2 . Let τ 1 have a period T 1 = T M , a computation time C 1 = C M , a relative deadline D 1 = T M , and a phasing ϕ 1 = ϕ M . Hence, task τ 1 consumes an initial amount C M from the capacity of β M in every period of β M , and the remainder ∆C M becomes available to task τ 2 . Now let task τ 2 have a period T 2 = T L , a computation time C 2 = ∆C L , a relative deadline D 2 = T L and a phasing ϕ 2 = ϕ L . Based on [6], C 2 can be at most ∆C L (T L ). As illustrated in Figure 9, ∆C L (T L ) < ∆C L (T L ) for T L ∈ (24, 37). As an example, let T 2 = 31 and C 2 = 5. According to our analysis, task τ 2 is schedulable, whereas according to [6] it is not. We therefore conclude that the schedulability analysis given in [6] is sufficient but not necessary.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we analysed the schedulability of CGBs within the context of fixed-priority preemptive scheduling (FPPS). Given additional resources requested by MIA, we described how to determine the worst-case amount of budget that can be conditionally guaranteed to LIA under arbitrary phasings of budgets of MIA and LIA. Our analysis is based on both best-case and worst-case analysis techniques. We complemented best-case analysis with similar techniques as have been developed previously for worstcase analysis, such as a technique to determine spare capacity [9]. We showed that because we use both best-case and worst-case techniques, it is not straightforward to base the analysis on a critical instant, and we therefore extended our analysis with a so-called cognac-glass algorithm (CGA). We concluded the analysis with a presentation of an efficient algorithm to determine the worst-case available CGB.

Given our analysis, we evaluated the effectiveness of CGBs, and concluded that CGBs are particularly useful for software video processing. Next, we explained that our analytical results need not be tight in general. Finally, we compared our approach with existing analysis techniques for hierarchical FPPS. Although our approach is pessimistic, we showed that it is less pessimistic than existing techniques. We concluded that best-case analysis techniques and a CGA are valuable extensions to the existing techniques, which we substantiated by means of an example.
